big_idea: Some sums are easy if I know a double or a make-ten. Mental strategies make math fast and accurate.
learning_intention: We are learning three mental math strategies for adding numbers up to 20: doubles, near-doubles, and make-ten.
student_learning_goal: I can use doubles, near-doubles, and make-ten to add numbers up to 20 in my head and explain how I did it.
success_criteria: I can name the double of any number from 1 to 10.
I can use a near-double to find a sum like 6+7.
I can use the make-ten strategy to find a sum like 8+5.
lesson_specific_materials: Anchor chart 'Mental Strategies' with 3 rows ready to fill: doubles, near-doubles, make-ten
Doubles the Robot poster (cameo character) at the front of the room
Lesson 2 mental-strategy tracker — provided in assessment_suite stage

minds_on.activity_name: Doubles the Robot Visits the Adding Machine
minds_on.hook: Doubles has TWO arms with the same number on each. What is double 6?
minds_on.teacher_script:
Bring children to the carpet. Reveal the Doubles the Robot poster. 'Friends — meet Doubles. Doubles is a special robot. Look at his arms. Both arms always show the SAME number.' Point to the robot's arms, each showing 4 dots. 'Both arms have 4. So Doubles is showing us a DOUBLE — 4 plus 4. What is 4 plus 4?'

Wait. 'Eight!' 'Yes — 8. Doubles makes adding easy because both addends are the same. Watch — I can ask you any double, and you can answer fast.' Run a quick chant: '1 plus 1?' '2!' '2 plus 2?' '4!' '3 plus 3?' '6!' Continue to 5+5. Most children will keep up. Add the doubles row to the anchor chart.

'Now Doubles has a friend who lives next door. The friend isn't a true double — but it's CLOSE.' Show: the robot's left arm has 4, the right arm has 5. 'This is a near-double. 4+5. How can we figure it out fast? Doubles already taught us that 4+4=8. So 4+5 is just ONE MORE than 8 — that's 9. We add 1 to the double to find the near-double.' Write the strategy: near-double = double + 1. Add the near-doubles row to the chart.

'And there's one MORE strategy Plus and Doubles want to show us today. It's called MAKE-TEN.' Show 8 red counters in the top ten-frame and 5 yellow counters in the bottom. '8 plus 5. Hmm — that's not a double, and it's not a near-double. But watch.' Move 2 yellow counters from the bottom up to fill the top frame to 10. 'Now I have 10 in the top frame and 3 in the bottom. 10 plus 3 — that's 13.' Write 8+5 = 8+2+3 = 10+3 = 13. 'See — I MOVED some yellows to MAKE TEN, and then I added what was left.' Add the make-ten row to the chart.

'Today we are going to PRACTISE all three strategies. By the end of class, you will pick the FASTEST strategy for any sum up to 20.'
student_actions: Listen as Doubles the Robot demonstrates true doubles.
Chant the doubles 1+1 through 5+5 with the class.
Predict the near-double 4+5 using the double 4+4.
Watch the make-ten move on the double ten-frame and echo the strategy.

steps.instruction: Whole group: do 5 doubles together rapid-fire (3+3, 5+5, 7+7, 4+4, 6+6). Then do 5 near-doubles together (3+4, 5+6, 6+7, 4+5, 8+9). Then do 3 make-tens together (8+5, 9+4, 7+6) using the double ten-frame.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Quick rapid-fire round. I say a double, you say the sum. Ready?' Run the doubles. 'Now I say a near-double, you say the strategy AND the sum. So if I say 6+7, you say six plus six is twelve plus one is thirteen. Ready?' Run the near-doubles. 'Now make-tens. I show 8+5 on the ten-frame. You walk me through the move.' Run the make-tens, slowing down for each child to verbalise the move.

steps.instruction: Set up the 3-station rotation. Station A: Doubles Dice — pair rolls one die, each names the double aloud, writes it. After 3 rounds, switch to two dice and find the near-double. Station B: Make-Ten Move — pair has the double ten-frame and counter cards. Draw a card with a sum like 8+5; build it; demonstrate the make-ten move; write the equation chain. Station C: Strategy Sort — pair has 12 fact cards. Sort them into 3 piles: doubles, near-doubles, make-ten. Some cards fit more than one — discuss why.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to students: 'Three stations, 7 minutes each. Listen for the chime to switch.' Set the rotation.

steps.instruction: Stretch challenge at Station C: include 2 cards that are 'count-on' facts (like 12+2). Pairs notice they don't fit any of the three strategies and need a fourth pile labeled count-on. This surfaces a Grade-1 truth: not every fact needs a fancy strategy — sometimes counting on is fastest.
steps.teacher_prompt: Say to pairs at Station C: 'You'll find some cards that DON'T fit any strategy. What strategy DO they need?' Lead pairs to the count-on idea: 12+2 = 12, 13, 14. Add count-on as a 4th row on the anchor chart.

steps.instruction: Circulate to record formative evidence on the mental-strategy tracker. Watch for: (a) does the child name a strategy before solving? (b) does the strategy match the fact (e.g., make-ten for 8+5, not for 3+3)? (c) can the child VERBALISE the strategy steps?
steps.teacher_prompt: Stop at each pair. Hand them a fact card. Ask 'Which strategy will you use?' BEFORE they solve. Mark the tracker for strategy choice and verbalisation.

differentiation.for_emerging: Children whose Lesson 1 fact recall is still emerging stay at Station A (Doubles Dice) for both rotations. Doubles are the easiest mental strategy to acquire because both addends are the same. Stay on doubles 1+1 to 5+5 only.
differentiation.for_extending: Stretch at Station C: include facts that go BEYOND 20 (e.g., 15+8). Discuss whether make-ten still works (yes — 15+8 = 15+5+3 = 20+3 = 23). This previews B2 Grade 2 territory.
differentiation.for_ell_or_iep: Provide a strategy poster card with picture supports — a 'twin' icon for doubles, a 'twin + 1' icon for near-doubles, a 10-shaped frame icon for make-ten. The icons reduce verbal load while preserving the strategy concept.
differentiation.for_movement_learners: Doubles dice naturally suits movement learners — the dice roll is kinesthetic. Allow the movement learner to STAND and use their body: hands up for two equal addends. For make-ten, let them physically pick up and move the counters.

formative_check.what_to_look_for: Three signals: (1) does the child select a strategy proactively (vs. just count-all on fingers)? (2) is the strategy match correct (doubles for 6+6, make-ten for 8+5)? (3) can the child explain the strategy in 1-2 sentences? Children who select AND match AND explain are at L4 for B2.3.
formative_check.how_to_record: Tick the mental-strategy tracker per child as you observe.

discussion_prompts: Which strategy felt the easiest today? Why?
If I asked you 7+8, which strategy would you use? Why?
Is there ever a time when count-on is the fastest? When?
What do you do when a sum doesn't fit any strategy?
consolidation.exit_routine: Each child whispers to a partner: 'My favourite strategy is ___ because ___.' Partners share a few examples with the class. Each child puts a sticky note with one fact and the strategy they'd use on the anchor chart on their way to the door.

assessment_in_this_lesson.evidence_collected: Strategy selection, strategy match, and strategy verbalisation across 3-5 facts per child observed during station rotations.
assessment_in_this_lesson.rationale: Lesson 2 is the keystone for B2.3. Children who can name AND match AND explain a strategy on Day 2 will move smoothly through Lesson 3 (subtraction strategies build on the same fact-family logic) and Lesson 4 (story-problem modelling). Children who can't yet select a strategy proactively need an extra small-group session before Lesson 4.

expanded_walkthrough.title: When the child uses make-ten correctly for 8+5 but defaults to count-all for 5+8 — repairing the 'order matters' make-ten misconception
expanded_walkthrough.rationale:
The most common Grade-1 trap on B2.3 (mental strategies to 20) is a subtle one: the child who has correctly learned the make-ten move STARTING FROM the larger addend, but cannot apply it when the larger addend is on the right. Given 5+8, they freeze — they try to move 5 to make 10 from the 5 side and discover that 5+8=13 doesn't have a clean make-ten path from the 5. The fix is to teach explicitly that make-ten works EITHER way: when you encounter 5+8, you can swap to 8+5 first (using Lesson 1's commutativity) and THEN make-ten.

This is a beautiful curriculum integration moment — Lesson 1 (B2.1: addition properties) is what unlocks Lesson 2 (B2.3: mental strategies). Without commutativity, make-ten is brittle. With it, make-ten works for any sum where one addend is 8 or 9.

The expanded walkthrough covers the precise moment when a child says 'I can't do 5+8' even though they can do 8+5 instantly. The repair takes 2 minutes and produces visible relief on the child's face — they suddenly see that the rule THEY learned in Lesson 1 (swap doesn't change the sum) is the KEY to making Lesson 2's strategy work everywhere.
expanded_walkthrough.setup: Pair is at Station B (Make-Ten Move). One child draws the card 5+8. They have just successfully done 8+5 using the make-ten move (moved 2 from the 5 side, got 10+3=13). They look at 5+8, freeze, and start finger-counting from 5: 'six, seven, eight, nine, ten, eleven, twelve, thirteen'. The teacher steps in.
expanded_walkthrough.teacher_script:
Crouch beside the child. 'You just did 8+5 perfectly with make-ten. Now the card says 5+8. Why are we counting on instead of making ten?' Wait. The child often says 'It's different.' or 'It's harder this way.' or just looks confused. 'Let me show you something.' Pull out two ten-frames, side-by-side. 'Show me 8+5 on these ten-frames.' The child puts 8 in the top, 5 in the bottom. Easy make-ten move.

'Now show me 5+8.' The child puts 5 in the top, 8 in the bottom. Note the visual: the top frame has 5 reds, the bottom has 8 yellows. 'Look at the counters. Are these THE SAME counters as 8+5?' The child looks. 'Yeah… same counters.' 'So is 5+8 the same TOTAL as 8+5?' '… yes.' 'And how did we figure out 8+5?' 'Make-ten.' 'So if 5+8 is the SAME total, we can use the SAME strategy. We just need to remember — order doesn't change the total. We learned that with Plus the Pup yesterday.'

Now the move: 'When I see 5+8, I think SWAP — make it 8+5 first. THEN I do make-ten.' Have the child do it. They put 8 in the top, 5 in the bottom, move 2 up, get 10+3=13. 'See? You did it the same way. The trick is — start with the bigger addend on the make-ten side.' Tick 'verbalise the strategy' on the tracker.

If the child STILL freezes when the order is reversed: the commutativity from Lesson 1 hasn't fully landed. Repair by going back to a fact-family triangle. Show the child the 5/8/13 triangle: 'This triangle has 5 and 8 at the bottom. The total is 13. It does NOT matter which addend is the first one we read. 5+8 and 8+5 are the same fact in the same triangle.' This Lesson-1 callback is what makes Lesson 2 stick.

Long-term recovery: every time a child uses make-ten in the next 3 days, ask them 'Did you have to swap first?' If yes, celebrate the swap as a strategy move. If no, ask 'Could you have used the swap?' Build the swap-first reflex over the week.
expected_student_responses: (Confused) Freezes on 5+8 even after doing 8+5 fluently. Sees the two as different problems. Most common at the start of Lesson 2 for transition learners.
(Mid) Eventually swaps after the teacher prompts. Doesn't yet auto-swap but recognises the move once it's named.
(Strong) Auto-swaps when the bigger addend is on the right. Says 'I'll swap to 8+5 then make-ten' before solving. Has internalised the Lesson 1 commutative property as a tool.

(Stretched) Volunteers an alternative: 'I can also make 5 into 5 — I mean, I can move 3 from the 8 to make the 5 into an 8, and then it's a double 8+5 wait that doesn't work.' The child is exploring strategy combinations. Affirm and redirect to the canonical make-ten move.
common_misconceptions: Make-ten only works when the bigger addend is on the left. (Order-dependence misconception. Repair: explicit swap-first move using fact-family triangles from Lesson 1.)

Doubles and near-doubles are the same thing. (Child uses 'doubles' loosely to mean 'two of something'. Repair: a TRUE double has both addends equal — 4+4. A near-double has one off — 4+5. Show side-by-side.)

If I can count to the answer, I don't need a strategy. (Child sees strategies as 'optional' rather than 'faster'. Repair: time them on 8+5 with count-all (12 sec) vs make-ten (3 sec). The time difference is the reason for the strategy.)
recovery_moves: Always say the swap aloud before doing make-ten. 'I see 5+8 — I'll swap to 8+5 — now I make ten.' Three sentences. Becomes automatic by Day 3.
Use fact-family triangles to reinforce that addend order is interchangeable. Lesson 1's anchor poster + Lesson 2's strategy chart together make the swap-first move stick.
Time the strategies. A timed comparison (count-all 12 sec, make-ten 3 sec) gives children a concrete reason to use the strategy. Without the time comparison, strategies feel like extra work.

worksheet_brief.purpose: Independent practice of B2.3 (mental strategies to 20). Captures formative evidence on strategy selection and execution.

parts_outline.task: Doubles row: child completes 8 doubles facts (1+1 through 8+8) in a fact-fluency table with answer boxes.
Near-doubles row: 6 near-doubles like 5+6, 7+8, 3+4. For each, the child writes the related double as a hint, then writes the sum.
Make-ten row: 4 make-ten problems on the double ten-frame. Each shows the starting position; the child draws the make-ten move (an arrow) and writes the equation chain.
Strategy choice: 4 sums (e.g., 6+6, 7+8, 9+5, 12+3). For each, the child circles the strategy they'd use (double / near-double / make-ten / count-on).

expected_image_assets: Doubles the Robot in the worksheet header
6 near-double pairs with hint slots for Part 2
4 double ten-frames with starting counters for Part 3
4 strategy-choice rows with strategy icons for Part 4
